items.topic: Longitudinal comparison of intrapulmonary cavities and air-fluid levels in Mounier-Kuhn syndrome

actions.observe: Compare Figure 7 (follow-up) vs Figure 1 (initial) for count and size of cystic/cavitary lucencies and presence of horizontal air-fluid levels.
actions.when: Question explicitly requests comparison between two timepoints (e.g., 'follow-up... compared to initial').
actions.stop: Visual confirmation of increased cavity burden and new air-fluid levels in the later image contradicts 'reduction' or 'stable' options.

items.avoid: Inferring disease progression or regression from chest_xray_classifier scores; assuming single-image report generator output reflects temporal change; overlooking air-fluid levels as a sign of active superinfection/progression.
items.source_evidence: Old model predicted 'Reduction in size and number... with no new air/fluid levels'. Correct answer is 'Increase in size and number... with new air/fluid levels visible'. Source Figure 7 shows markedly more extensive cystic changes and distinct air-fluid levels compared to Figure 1. Classifier returned no strong findings for both, proving it cannot track this specific morphological progression. Report generator withheld temporal clauses, confirming it cannot support interval assessment.

items.topic: Post-pneumonectomy cardiac herniation and mediastinal shift

actions.observe: Compare cardiac silhouette position relative to midline and spine in Figure 1a vs 1b; check for rightward displacement into empty hemithorax and loss of normal left heart border contour.
actions.when: Question references paired post-op CXRs (Fig 1a/1b) and acute hemodynamic instability after right-sided thoracic surgery.
actions.stop: Clear rightward cardiac shift with mediastinal deviation into right pleural space is visible in Fig 1b compared to baseline Fig 1a.

actions.observe: Assess right hemithorax for absence of lung markings and presence of cardiac shadow occupying the space, confirming herniation rather than effusion or mass.
actions.when: Cardiac silhouette appears abnormally positioned toward right side in follow-up image.
actions.stop: Heart轮廓 clearly extends beyond expected mediastinal boundaries into right thoracic cavity without fluid level or discrete mass.

items.avoid: Do not infer tamponade, hemorrhage, or atelectasis solely from enlarged cardiomediastinum classifier score; do not assume resolution if only one image shows abnormality without explicit temporal binding.
items.source_evidence: Old model claimed 'Cardiac volvulus' but correct answer is 'Cardiac herniation'. Source images show heart displaced into right pleural cavity in Fig 1b vs normal position in Fig 1a. Classifier flagged 'Enlarged Cardiomediastinum' but this is nonspecific; visual comparison confirms structural displacement, not volume increase. Uncertainty arises when timepoints are unbound or tools misinterpret size change as pathology instead of positional shift.

items.topic: Anterior mediastinal mass localization and malignancy signs on CXR

actions.observe: PA view: Assess if the mass obscures the ascending aorta or right heart border (anterior) vs descending aorta/spine (posterior). Check for lobulated/ill-defined margins and bilateral pleural effusions.
actions.when: Evaluating mediastinal mass characteristics and location
actions.stop: Mass location (anterior/posterior), margin definition (smooth/lobulated), and presence of effusions are visually confirmed.

actions.observe: Lateral view: Verify mass projects over the retrosternal clear space (anterior) or paraspinal region (posterior). Confirm sternotomy wires are present but do not obscure the mass assessment.
actions.when: Confirming anterior location suggested by PA view
actions.stop: Anterior projection in retrosternal space is verified on lateral view.

items.avoid: Relying on classifier scores for severity or report generator text which contradicts image findings (e.g., claiming pneumonia when mass is evident). Do not assume smooth margins imply benignity if lobulation/effusions are present.
items.source_evidence: Old model claims varied between 'pneumonia' and 'mass'. Correct answer identifies an anteriorly located, lobulated mass with ill-defined margins and bibasal pleural effusions, consistent with thymic carcinoma. Visual evidence on PA shows a widened superior mediastinum with lobulated contours obscuring anterior structures and blunted costophrenic angles. Lateral view confirms anterior projection. Classifier score (0.93) supports mass presence but lacks specificity; report generator hallucinated pneumonia. Direct visual inspection of margins and effusions is required to distinguish malignant thymic carcinoma from benign cysts or lymphoma.

items.topic: Congenital bronchial atresia: tubular opacity and hyperlucency

actions.observe: Left upper lobe for a branching or tubular soft-tissue density (mucocoele) adjacent to an area of increased radiolucency (hyperlucency/air trapping).
actions.when: Question describes a persistent tubular opacity with surrounding hyperlucency in the LUL.
actions.stop: Visual confirmation of the specific combination of a tubular/finger-in-glove opacity and adjacent hyperlucent lung parenchyma.

actions.observe: Verify the opacity is tubular/branching rather than a round cyst or cavitary lesion, and check for absence of acute infectious signs like consolidation.
actions.when: Differentiating from ABPA (usually bilateral/central), sequestration (mass-like), or infection.
actions.stop: Identification of the classic mucocoele morphology excludes cystic or cavitary alternatives.

items.avoid: Relying on chest_xray_classifier scores (normalized XRV, not probabilities) or chest_xray_report_generator outputs (which may falsely report 'clear lungs' for subtle congenital anomalies). Do not assume 'no strong finding' implies normality.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions correctly identified 'Left upper lobe segmental bronchial atresia' / 'Congenital bronchial atresia'. Tool observations showed 'strong_findings: {}' and reports stating 'lungs are clear', contradicting the visible pathology. The correction relies on visually identifying the specific triad of LUL location, tubular opacity (mucocoele), and surrounding hyperlucency, which automated tools failed to detect or report accurately.

items.topic: Sarcoidosis CXR pattern recognition: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and peribronchovascular nodules

actions.observe: Bilateral hilar regions for symmetric enlargement and lung parenchyma for small nodules tracking along bronchovascular bundles (perilymphatic distribution).
actions.when: Evaluating options for sarcoidosis vs other granulomatous or neoplastic diseases.
actions.stop: Confirmation of bilateral hilar adenopathy combined with peribronchovascular nodularity supports the diagnosis; absence of cavitation or unilateral dominance rules out TB/malignancy.

actions.observe: Verify symmetry of hilar contours and check for 'galaxy sign' (conglomerate nodules) if mentioned in options.
actions.when: Visual assessment of nodule distribution is ambiguous or requires confirmation of perilymphatic pattern.
actions.stop: Expert confirms bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and peribronchovascular nodules consistent with sarcoidosis.

items.avoid: Relying on the chest_xray_classifier 'Mass' score (0.85) as evidence of a solitary mass or malignancy; this score likely reflects the conglomerate nodal masses of sarcoidosis. Do not trust the report generator's claim of 'normal hilar contours' which contradicts the visible pathology.
items.source_evidence: The previous answer correctly identified 'Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with multiple small nodules along the peribronchovascular bundles'. The chest_xray_classifier incorrectly flagged a 'Mass' (0.85), likely misinterpreting the bilateral hilar adenopathy/nodules as a single mass. The report generator falsely reported 'normal hilar and mediastinal contours', contradicting the obvious radiographic findings. The skill is to visually confirm the specific sarcoid pattern (BHL + perilymphatic nodules) despite misleading tool outputs.

items.topic: Stage I sarcoidosis lymph node pattern recognition

actions.observe: Bilateral hilar regions for symmetric, well-defined lobulated enlargement; check right paratracheal stripe for concomitant adenopathy.
actions.when: Question asks to characterize lymphadenopathy pattern or stage sarcoidosis based on CXR findings.
actions.stop: Symmetry of hilar nodes and presence/absence of paratracheal involvement are visually confirmed.

actions.observe: Lung parenchyma for absence of focal consolidation, opacities, or fibrosis to distinguish Stage I from Stage II/III.
actions.when: Differentiating Stage I (nodes only) from advanced stages or infectious/malignant mimics.
actions.stop: Clear lung fields confirm isolated nodal disease consistent with Stage I.

items.avoid: Relying on classifier 'Mass' scores as probability or severity; assuming report generator's 'normal silhouette' negates visible hilar fullness; inferring asymmetry or calcification without direct visual confirmation.
items.source_evidence: Old model claims relied on tool outputs (classifier score 0.88 for Mass, report stating normal silhouette) which failed to capture the specific nodal pattern. Released correct answers consistently identify 'bilateral symmetric hilar lymph node enlargement' often with 'paratracheal enlargement' as key to Stage I sarcoidosis. Visual evidence in Figure 1a shows distinct bilateral hilar fullness with preserved lung fields, contradicting the generic 'normal' report and requiring direct inspection of nodal symmetry and margins rather than automated scores.

items.topic: Azygos lobe luxation and teardrop opacity absence post-pneumothorax

actions.observe: Right upper lung zone for the azygos fissure line and the caudal end of the fissure to check for the presence or absence of the teardrop-shaped azygos vein opacity.
actions.when: Question asks about changes in azygos lobe/fissure appearance following pneumothorax or reexpansion.
actions.stop: Visual confirmation of whether the teardrop opacity is present at the fissure base or if the fissure appears empty/vein displaced medially.

actions.observe: Medial aspect of the right upper lung apex to identify if the azygos vein has shifted medially (luxation) away from its normal position at the fissure base.
actions.when: Teardrop opacity is absent at the expected fissure location.
actions.stop: Identification of the azygos vein in a paramediastinal or medial position confirms luxation.

items.avoid: Assuming the azygos fissure is unchanged or the teardrop opacity persists when the vein has luxated; relying on single-image report generators that cannot assess temporal changes or specific anatomical variants like azygos lobes without explicit prompting.
items.source_evidence: Old model claims often failed to recognize the absence of the teardrop opacity or misinterpreted the fissure status. Released corrections consistently identify that following pneumothorax/reexpansion, the azygos fissure appears empty and the teardrop-shaped opacity (azygos vein) is no longer visible at its lower end due to medial displacement (luxation). Source images show the CT (Fig 1a) with the vein in the fissure and CXR (Fig 3a) where the arrow points to the fissure but the typical teardrop density is absent/displaced, confirming the 'empty fissure' sign of luxation.

items.topic: Large right lower hemithorax mass with mass effect

actions.observe: Right lower hemithorax opacity extent and margins; check for diaphragm depression and mediastinal/tracheal shift to the left.
actions.when: Evaluating a large unilateral chest mass for size and mass effect.
actions.stop: Mass location confirmed in lower right hemithorax with visible downward displacement of the right hemidiaphragm and leftward mediastinal shift.

actions.observe: Compare automated report findings against visual evidence of mass effect.
actions.when: Automated tools describe 'clear lungs' or 'unremarkable mediastinum' despite obvious large opacity.
actions.stop: Visual confirmation of large mass contradicts tool output; prioritize direct image inspection over generated text.

items.avoid: Accepting automated reports stating 'lungs are clear' or 'no focal consolidation' when a large mass is visually present; assuming small size based on lack of classifier confidence scores.
items.source_evidence: Previous answer incorrectly described the mass as 'small' and 'benign' requiring monitoring. Reference answer corrects this to 'large', occupying the lower right hemithorax, likely a giant solitary fibrous tumour requiring resection due to mass effect (diaphragm down, mediastinum left). Tool observations falsely reported 'clear lungs' and 'unremarkable mediastinum', demonstrating that automated classifiers/reports can miss large masses; visual inspection of mass effect is required.

items.topic: Differentiating adenocarcinoma from pneumonia in lobar consolidation

actions.observe: Right upper lobe opacity margins and internal texture; specifically check for sharp fissural boundaries combined with visible air bronchograms (dark branching lines within white opacity).
actions.when: Evaluating a homogeneous lobar opacity that respects anatomical boundaries.
actions.stop: Confirmation of air bronchograms within a sharply demarcated lobar opacity supports adenocarcinoma over typical fluffy pneumonia.

actions.observe: Lung volume and mediastinal position relative to the opacity to assess for mass effect or atelectasis.
actions.when: Opacity is confirmed to respect the fissure.
actions.stop: Absence of significant volume loss helps distinguish this neoplastic consolidation from obstructive atelectasis.

items.avoid: Assuming that 'lobar consolidation respecting the fissure' automatically indicates infectious pneumonia; ignoring air bronchograms as a sign of patency often seen in mucinous adenocarcinoma.
items.source_evidence: Old models consistently predicted 'Infectious pneumonia' based on the lobar distribution and fissure respect. The released correct answer is 'Pulmonary adenocarcinoma'. Source observations confirm the opacity is homogeneous, respects the fissure, and contains air bronchograms. This specific combination (sharp margins + patent airways) mimics pneumonia but indicates neoplasm when clinical context or persistence suggests otherwise.

items.topic: Healed varicella pneumonia: calcified nodules with random distribution

actions.observe: Inspect lung fields for multiple small (1-3mm) nodular opacities with random distribution and high density suggesting calcification.
actions.when: Evaluating diffuse nodular patterns to distinguish healed VZV from miliary TB or metastases.
actions.stop: Calcified nodules with random distribution are confirmed; absence of cavitation or spiculation supports healed etiology.

actions.observe: Verify absence of cavitary lesions, spiculated margins, or bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy to rule out active TB, malignancy, or sarcoidosis.
actions.when: Differentiating calcified nodules from other differential diagnoses listed in options.
actions.stop: No features of active infection or malignancy are present alongside the calcified nodules.

items.avoid: Do not rely on chest_xray_classifier scores (normalized XRV, not probabilities) or single-image report generator outputs which may miss subtle calcifications or falsely report effusions/consolidation absent in pixels.
items.source_evidence: Old model claims relied on classifier/report tools that failed to identify specific nodule characteristics. Released correct answers consistently identify 'healed varicella zoster virus pneumonia' based on 'calcified nodules' and 'random distribution'. Source image shows faint, dense, randomly distributed micronodules consistent with this diagnosis, contradicting tool reports of 'no focal consolidation' or 'small bilateral pleural effusions'.

items.topic: Longitudinal assessment of right lower lobe atelectasis and mediastinal shift on serial CXR

actions.observe: Compare right lower lobe opacity density and volume between the earliest and latest CXR; check for increasing silhouetting of the right hemidiaphragm and rightward mediastinal/tracheal shift indicating progressive collapse.
actions.when: Question asks about progression or change over time using multiple images.
actions.stop: Visual confirmation of worsening RLL opacity with associated volume loss signs (diaphragm elevation, mediastinal shift) across the time series.

actions.observe: Verify that the question explicitly binds timepoints to specific images (e.g., 'initial', 'later') before asserting chronology; do not rely on file order or single-image tool reports.
actions.when: Evaluating temporal changes in pathology.
actions.stop: Timepoint binding is confirmed in the question text or image labels; otherwise report uncertainty regarding progression.

items.avoid: Inferring disease progression from differences in chest_xray_classifier scores or relying on chest_xray_report_generator for temporal claims, as it processes single images without chronological context.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions correctly identified progressive RLL atelectasis due to foreign body but relied on tools that cannot validate chronology. The classifier provides non-calibrated scores, and the report generator lacks temporal awareness. Correct answer requires direct visual comparison of serial CXRs (Figures 4 and 5) to confirm increasing opacity and volume loss, independent of tool outputs.

items.topic: PAVM nodule morphology and margin characterization

actions.observe: Right upper lobe apex for a solitary nodule; specifically assess if margins are sharp/well-defined versus indistinct/spiculated, and if shape is round/smooth versus irregular/lobulated.
actions.when: Question asks to characterize a nodule's shape/margins to support or refute PAVM diagnosis.
actions.stop: Nodule is visualized and its margin definition (sharp vs indistinct) and shape (round vs irregular) are clearly determined.

actions.observe: Verify the nodule is solitary and lacks associated consolidation, cavitation, or calcification which might suggest alternative diagnoses like granuloma or malignancy.
actions.when: Differentiating PAVM from other nodular etiologies based on isolated appearance.
actions.stop: Absence of secondary features (calcification, satellite lesions) confirms solitary nature consistent with vascular malformation.

items.avoid: Assuming that 'round and smooth' margins exclude PAVM; source evidence indicates PAVM can present with sharp margins and may be described as irregular in specific contexts or options, contradicting the heuristic that only smooth/round nodules are benign or vascular.
items.source_evidence: Old model predicted 'round and smooth with sharp margins is inconsistent with PAVM'. Reference answer corrected this to 'irregularly shaped with sharp margins, supporting PAVM' (Source 15697_8353800559211). Other sources (15697_8353800645590) also link 'sharp edges' to solitary PAVM. The key learning is that sharp margins support PAVM, and the shape descriptor 'irregular' was the correct discriminator in the specific multiple-choice context provided, overriding the assumption that PAVMs must be perfectly round/smooth to be identified as such against malignant mimics.

items.topic: EGPA vs CEP: Apical peripheral opacities

actions.observe: Upper lung zones (apices) on PA view for subtle peripheral/pleural-based opacities distinct from central/hilar regions.
actions.when: Question asks to distinguish EGPA from Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia or Sarcoidosis based on opacity distribution.
actions.stop: Confirming apical peripheral opacities supports EGPA; confirming lower lobe peripheral opacities supports CEP.

actions.observe: Lateral view to verify if upper zone opacities are truly peripheral (abutting pleura) versus central/perihilar.
actions.when: PA view shows upper zone density but zonal distribution (central vs peripheral) is ambiguous.
actions.stop: Peripheral location in upper zones confirmed; central location suggests alternative diagnosis.

items.avoid: Assuming peripheral opacities imply Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia (CEP) without checking vertical distribution; CEP typically affects lower/mid zones, whereas EGPA favors apices. Do not rely on classifier scores for this subtle pattern.
items.source_evidence: Old models frequently selected 'Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia' or 'Central opacities' despite the reference answer being EGPA. The correction relies on identifying 'peripheral opacities with apical predominance'. Source images (Fig 1a/1b) show subtle densities in the upper lobes near the pleura, distinguishing them from the basal predominance of CEP or the hilar/central distribution of sarcoidosis. Clinical history of asthma/polyposis is a necessary context term.

items.topic: Identifying bilateral consolidation patterns and absence of pleural effusion in COVID-19 pneumonia

actions.observe: Right upper lobe for sharply defined consolidation bounded by the fissure and left lower zone for additional opacity.
actions.when: Evaluating options describing specific lobar involvement versus diffuse or cavitary patterns.
actions.stop: When RUL fissure-defined consolidation and LLL opacity are visually confirmed.

actions.observe: Costophrenic angles and lateral lung margins for blunting or meniscus sign indicating pleural effusion.
actions.when: Distinguishing between options that include pleural effusion and those that explicitly exclude it.
actions.stop: When costophrenic angles are sharp and no fluid levels are visible.

items.avoid: Relying on automated report generators that may falsely claim 'grossly clear' lungs due to body habitus limitations, or assuming 'no strong finding' from classifiers implies normality.
items.source_evidence: Previous model predictions and tool outputs (classifier/report generator) incorrectly suggested clear lungs or non-specific findings. The released correct answer identifies specific RUL consolidation at the fissure and LLL consolidation without effusion. Visual inspection confirms these opacities despite technical limitations, contradicting the 'clear' tool reports.

items.topic: Differentiating pulmonary contusion from viral GGO based on opacity morphology and distribution

actions.observe: Inspect the right lung base for opacity characteristics: distinguish ill-defined, peripheral ground-glass opacities (viral) from dense, non-segmental consolidations conforming to impact site (contusion).
actions.when: Question provides history of trauma/syncope but asks for diagnosis based on CXR findings.
actions.stop: When opacity is confirmed as peripheral/ill-defined GGO rather than focal consolidation at injury site.

actions.observe: Verify absence of rib fractures or other osseous trauma signs that would strongly support pulmonary contusion over incidental viral finding.
actions.when: Evaluating traumatic etiology vs infectious etiology in context of syncope/fall history.
actions.stop: When skeletal survey confirms intact ribs despite soft tissue opacity.

items.avoid: Assuming right-sided opacity equals traumatic contusion solely due to mentioned history of syncope/trauma; ignoring that asymptomatic COVID-19 can present with unilateral peripheral GGOs indistinguishable from early contusion without specific morphological cues.
items.source_evidence: Old model predicted 'Pulmonary contusion' based on trauma history. Reference answer corrected to 'Asymptomatic COVID-19'. Source image shows ill-defined, patchy ground-glass opacities in the right lung base/periphery (circled), lacking the dense, homogeneous consolidation typical of contusion. The error stems from over-weighting clinical history (trauma) over radiographic phenotype (peripheral GGO).

items.topic: Longitudinal assessment of lung opacity progression and new contralateral findings

actions.observe: Compare the density and extent of the right middle/lower lobe opacity between the initial (Figure 1a) and follow-up (Figure 4) images to determine if it has increased, decreased, or remained stable.
actions.when: Question asks for disease progression over a specific time period involving multiple images.
actions.stop: Visual comparison confirms whether the primary opacity has changed in size/density and if new opacities have appeared in the contralateral lung.

actions.observe: Inspect the left lung field in the follow-up image (Figure 4) specifically for new opacities that were absent in the baseline image (Figure 1a).
actions.when: Evaluating options regarding new findings or spread of disease.
actions.stop: Presence or absence of new left-sided opacities is visually confirmed against the baseline.

items.avoid: Inferring disease progression or severity changes based on differences in chest_xray_classifier scores (e.g., 0.88 vs 0.89), as these are uncalibrated normalized scores and not longitudinal metrics. Do not assume resolution or stability without direct visual comparison of the paired images.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions incorrectly suggested resolving pneumonia or cryptogenic organizing pneumonia based on flawed interpretation or lack of temporal binding. The released correct answer identifies progression of right lung opacity and new left lung opacities (adenocarcinoma in situ). Source evidence requires direct visual comparison of Figure 1a (baseline homogeneous RML opacity) and Figure 4 (increased RML density + new left lung opacity). Classifier scores provided in observations (0.88 vs 0.89) are explicitly noted as not being severity measurements; relying on them leads to incorrect conclusions about stability or change.

items.topic: Longitudinal assessment of residual atelectasis location in resolving pneumonia

actions.observe: Compare the basal lung zones in the initial vs discharge images to identify the specific side (left vs right) where linear opacities or atelectatic streaks persist after the resolution of peripheral consolidations.
actions.when: Question asks for evolution of findings and specifies residual signs like atelectasis at a specific timepoint (e.g., discharge).
actions.stop: When the side of the residual basal opacity is visually confirmed and matched against the options.

items.avoid: Assuming bilateral symmetry in residual findings or misidentifying the side of atelectasis due to poor contrast; do not rely on classifier scores for longitudinal change.
items.source_evidence: The model previously selected 'right basal zone' for residual atelectasis, but the correct answer is 'left basal zone'. The source images (Figure 14/15 context) show that while peripheral consolidations improve, thin linear opacities remain specifically in the left base. This requires direct visual comparison of the basal regions across timepoints rather than general impression of improvement.

items.topic: Detecting pneumothorax via lung edge and peripheral lucency in paired CXR

actions.observe: Compare the right hemithorax between Figure 1 and Figure 2. Specifically inspect the lateral and apical regions for a new visible visceral pleural line (lung edge) separated from the chest wall by a lucent space devoid of lung markings.
actions.when: Question describes sudden worsening, pleuritic pain, or asks to explain interval changes between two specific X-rays.
actions.stop: A distinct visceral pleural line with absent peripheral vascular markings is identified in the follow-up image compared to baseline.

actions.observe: Assess for signs of tension or volume loss if pneumothorax is suspected: check for mediastinal shift away from the affected side, depression of the hemidiaphragm, or increased intercostal spaces on the symptomatic side.
actions.when: A potential pneumothorax line is observed or clinical symptoms suggest significant pressure.
actions.stop: Mediastinal position and diaphragm contour are evaluated relative to the baseline image to determine severity.

items.avoid: Mistaking the skin fold or scapular edge for a pneumothorax line; assuming opacity progression explains sudden pain without ruling out air; relying on classifier scores which do not detect pneumothorax reliably.
items.source_evidence: Old models frequently selected 'Progression of COVID-19 pneumonia' or 'Bacterial superinfection' based on general opacity patterns. The correct answer is 'Development of a right-sided pneumothorax'. Visual evidence in Figure 2 shows a new lucency in the right upper/lateral zone with a visible lung edge not present in Figure 1, correlating with sudden pain and crackles (likely atelectasis/compression). The skill requires direct visual comparison of the lung periphery rather than global density assessment.

items.topic: Posterior mediastinal mass identification via paraspinal line displacement

actions.observe: Inspect the lower thoracic spine region on the PA view to trace the right and left paraspinal lines. Look for lateral deviation or obliteration of these vertical lines adjacent to the vertebral bodies, indicating a soft tissue mass in the posterior mediastinum.
actions.when: Evaluating options describing mediastinal widening or paraspinal line displacement.
actions.stop: When bilateral lateral displacement of the paraspinal lines is confirmed visually, distinguishing it from unilateral displacement or normal anatomy.

actions.observe: Verify the integrity of the vertebral bodies adjacent to the paraspinal opacity. Check for bone destruction (suggesting metastasis/abscess) versus smooth margins with preserved bone (suggesting lymphoma/neurogenic tumor).
actions.when: Differentiating between malignant invasion and soft tissue masses like lymphoma.
actions.stop: When vertebral endplates appear intact despite significant soft tissue widening.

items.avoid: Relying on automated report generators that may describe the mediastinum as 'unremarkable' despite visible paraspinal widening, or assuming unilateral displacement implies neurogenic tumor without verifying the contralateral side.
items.source_evidence: The model previously selected Option A (unilateral right displacement/neurogenic tumor) or claimed no displacement, while the correct answer (Option B) identified bilateral lateral displacement of paraspinal lines suggesting lymphoma. Visual inspection of Figure 1b (annotated) confirms arrows pointing to lateral displacement of both right and left paraspinal lines in the lower mediastinum. The error stemmed from failing to detect the subtle bilateral nature of the posterior mediastinal mass and misinterpreting the specific radiological sign.

items.topic: Septic pulmonary emboli: cavitating nodules and asymmetric pleural effusion

actions.observe: Bilateral lung fields for multiple nodular opacities; specifically inspect centers for lucency (cavitation) and distribution (peripheral/hematogenous).
actions.when: Evaluating options distinguishing septic emboli from non-cavitating nodules or single lesions.
actions.stop: Presence of multiple bilateral cavitating nodules is confirmed visually.

actions.observe: Costophrenic angles and hemidiaphragms to compare pleural fluid volume; verify if left-sided effusion is moderate/larger than right.
actions.when: Differentiating between symmetric/asymmetric effusion or significant/minimal fluid descriptions.
actions.stop: Asymmetry (Left > Right) and severity (moderate vs minimal) are established.

items.avoid: Relying on the report generator's 'no evidence of pneumonia' impression, which contradicts the visible cavitating nodules and effusion; do not assume uniform nodule appearance or symmetric effusion without direct verification.
items.source_evidence: Old model claims and tool outputs (classifier score 0.8, report stating 'no pneumonia') failed to identify specific pathology. Released correct answers consistently describe 'several cavitating nodules bilaterally' with 'moderate left-sided and minimal right-sided pleural effusion'. Visual inspection of Figure 1 confirms these findings: arrows point to peripheral nodules with central lucency (cavitation) and blunting of the left costophrenic angle greater than the right. The skill is to prioritize direct visual confirmation of cavitation and effusion asymmetry over contradictory automated text reports.

items.topic: Diaphragmatic contour abnormalities: elevation vs scalloping in lymphangioma

actions.observe: Right hemidiaphragm dome position relative to left and costophrenic angle sharpness; inspect for smooth upward displacement without blunting.
actions.when: Evaluating options distinguishing diaphragmatic elevation causes (mass effect vs paralysis vs effusion).
actions.stop: When right dome is clearly elevated with preserved sharp costophrenic angle, ruling out pleural effusion.

actions.observe: Left hemidiaphragm contour for irregularity, undulation, or scalloping along the superior margin.
actions.when: Differentiating lymphangioma (scalloping) from simple elevation or hernia.
actions.stop: When distinct scalloped/wavy contour is identified on the left side, supporting cystic/lymphatic etiology.

actions.observe: Absence of meniscus sign or homogeneous basal opacity obscuring the diaphragm.
actions.when: Excluding pleural effusion as cause of apparent elevation.
actions.stop: When lung base remains aerated down to the elevated diaphragm line, confirming mass effect rather than fluid.

items.avoid: Assuming diaphragmatic elevation implies paralysis or hepatomegaly without checking for concurrent contralateral scalloping; mistaking cystic mass effect for pleural effusion due to basal opacity.
items.source_evidence: Old models frequently selected diaphragmatic paralysis, hepatomegaly, or pleural effusion. The released correct answer identifies lymphangioma based on the specific combination of right hemidiaphragm elevation (mass compression) and left hemidiaphragm scalloping. Visual evidence shows a high right dome with sharp CP angle (no effusion) and an irregular, wavy left diaphragm contour. Tools failed to detect these morphological nuances, returning generic 'no pneumonia' reports.

items.topic: Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome vs Hypogenetic lung syndrome differentiation via hyperlucency and vascular markings

actions.observe: Compare the right hemithorax to the left for unilateral hyperlucency (increased radiolucency) and assess the density/number of pulmonary vascular markings in the hyperlucent area.
actions.when: Evaluating a patient with history of recurrent infections presenting with asymmetric lung findings.
actions.stop: When unilateral hyperlucency is confirmed alongside visibly diminished or absent pulmonary vessels on the affected side, distinguishing it from simple overinflation or effusion.

actions.observe: Inspect the hilum on the hyperlucent side for size; specifically check if it appears smaller or hypoplastic compared to the contralateral side.
actions.when: Differentiating Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome (small hilum) from Congenital Lobar Overinflation (often normal or displaced hilum) or Unilateral Absence of Pulmonary Artery.
actions.stop: Once hilar asymmetry is established in conjunction with parenchymal hyperlucency.

items.avoid: Relying on automated report generators that may hallucinate pneumothorax or atelectasis in hyperlucent lungs, or assuming 'no strong finding' from classifiers implies normality when subtle vascular paucity is present.
items.source_evidence: Old models incorrectly predicted Hypogenetic lung syndrome. The reference answer is Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome, supported by the specific combination of right hemithorax hyperlucency and vessel paucity consistent with recurrent infection history. Tool observations were unreliable (report generator claimed pneumothorax/atelectasis not supported by visual evidence of SJMS features). The key discriminant is the visual presence of hyperlucency with reduced vascularity rather than volume loss or absence of structures seen in other syndromes.

items.topic: Differentiating haemothorax from parapneumonic effusion via rib anomalies

actions.observe: Left hemithorax ribs and costophrenic angle for bony spurs, fractures, or irregularities adjacent to the pleural opacity
actions.when: Evaluating unilateral pleural effusion with chest pain to distinguish traumatic/haemorrhagic causes from infectious consolidation
actions.stop: Visible rib abnormality (e.g., spur) confirms mechanical cause; absence of bone defect supports inflammatory/infectious etiology

actions.observe: Density homogeneity of the left pleural opacity compared to typical fluid levels
actions.when: Assessing if effusion characteristics suggest blood (inhomogeneous/dense) vs simple fluid
actions.stop: Inhomogeneous density combined with rib anomaly strongly suggests haemothorax; uniform density suggests transudate/exudate

items.avoid: Assuming fever and effusion automatically indicate pneumonia without ruling out osseous trauma sources; relying on classifier 'no strong finding' as proof of normal ribs
items.source_evidence: Old model predicted 'Left-sided pneumonia leading to parapneumonic effusion' based on fever/pain history. Released correction identified 'Haemothorax caused by spontaneous rib spur rupture'. Source trajectory 18592_8143559034730 explicitly links the effusion to visible rib abnormalities. The error stems from overlooking subtle bony pathology (rib spur) in favor of common clinical associations (fever=pneumonia), despite the X-ray showing a large left effusion where a rib anomaly was present.

items.topic: Scimitar syndrome radiographic triad: anomalous vein, volume loss, diaphragm elevation

actions.observe: Right lower lung zone for a curvilinear tubular opacity (scimitar sign) paralleling the right heart border and descending toward the diaphragm.
actions.when: Question asks to identify findings supporting scimitar syndrome or locate the anomalous vein.
actions.stop: Curved shadow is clearly visualized adjacent to the right cardiac silhouette.

actions.observe: Right hemidiaphragm position relative to the left, and mediastinal/tracheal shift direction to assess for right-sided volume loss.
actions.when: Options distinguish between right vs left pathology or attribute cause of shift/elevation.
actions.stop: Right hemidiaphragm is visibly elevated compared to the left AND mediastinum is shifted toward the right.

items.avoid: Misidentifying the scimitar vein as being on the left side or attributing the mediastinal shift to left lung hyperinflation; do not rely on automated reports that miss the subtle curved vascular shadow.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions correctly identified the 'curved shadow near the right heart border' and 'right lung volume loss with right mediastinal shift and elevated right hemidiaphragm' as key features. Tool observations (report generator/classifier) failed to detect these specific signs, labeling the study limited or normal. The correction relies on direct visual confirmation of the right-sided anomalous vein and associated hypoplasia signs (elevated right diaphragm, ipsilateral shift), which are pathognomonic for scimitar syndrome.

items.topic: Distinguishing lung-to-breast metastasis from primary breast cancer via mass location and morphology on CXR

actions.observe: Inspect the right lower hemithorax for a well-circumscribed, lobulated opacity. Determine if it lies within the lung parenchyma (medial/deep) or projects over the soft tissue of the breast/chest wall (lateral/superficial).
actions.when: Evaluating options distinguishing primary breast carcinoma from lung metastasis to the chest wall.
actions.stop: When the mass is confirmed as a discrete, lobulated nodule located in the lower right lung field, supporting lung origin with secondary chest wall involvement.

actions.observe: Check for adherence to the thoracic fascia or infiltration into the chest wall soft tissues versus a distinct pulmonary nodule silhouette.
actions.when: Differentiating between Option A (primary breast/fascia adherence) and Option B/C (lung metastasis/lower lung position).
actions.stop: When visual evidence confirms the mass is primarily intrapulmonary (lower lobe) rather than a chest wall mass invading inward.

items.avoid: Assuming that a mass projecting over the breast shadow is automatically a primary breast tumor; do not infer 'clear lungs' from automated report generators when a distinct focal nodule is visible in the lower zone.
items.source_evidence: Old models frequently misidentified the lesion as a primary breast carcinoma or failed to recognize the specific 'well-circumscribed, lobulated' morphology in the lower right lung. The released correct answers consistently identify the finding as a metastasis from the lung to the breast/chest wall based on its position in the lower right lung region. Visual inspection of Figure 2 confirms a distinct, lobulated opacity in the right lower lung field (indicated by arrow), which contradicts reports stating 'lungs are clear' and supports the diagnosis of a lung primary with metastatic spread rather than a primary breast tumor.

items.topic: Esophageal perforation complications: distinguishing pneumothorax from pleural effusion/mediastinitis on CXR

actions.observe: Right costophrenic angle and right hemithorax base for blunting or homogeneous opacity indicating pleural effusion; inspect mediastinal contours for widening or air suggesting abscess/mediastinitis.
actions.when: Evaluating esophageal perforation complications where pneumothorax was incorrectly predicted over effusion.
actions.stop: Clear visualization of right-sided fluid level/blunting confirms effusion; absence of visceral pleural line rules out pneumothorax.

actions.observe: Mediastinal width and paratracheal regions for soft tissue density or gas bubbles indicative of mediastinal abscess secondary to perforation.
actions.when: Visual inspection of mediastinum is equivocal due to overlapping structures or poor contrast.
actions.stop: Segmentation highlights abnormal mediastinal mass or fluid collection distinct from vascular shadows.

items.avoid: Assuming pneumothorax is the primary complication of esophageal perforation without visual evidence of a visceral pleural line; overlooking right-sided pleural effusion as a sign of mediastinal leakage.
items.source_evidence: Old model predicted 'Pneumothorax due to oesophageal perforation' based on clinical history but missed radiographic signs. Reference answer is 'Right-sided pleural effusion associated with mediastinal abscess'. Source Figure 2 (CXR) shows right basal opacity consistent with effusion, not pneumothorax. Figure 1a (CT) confirms mediastinal pathology. The error stems from prioritizing mechanism (perforation -> air) over actual image findings (fluid/abscess). Skill: Verify presence of effusion vs pneumothorax specifically in perforation cases.

items.topic: Longitudinal assessment of pulmonary edema resolution in aspiration

actions.observe: Inspect Figure 1 for bilateral perihilar fluffy opacities with peripheral sparing (bat-wing pattern) indicative of pulmonary edema/aspiration.
actions.when: Question asks to describe findings in the first image of a pair.
actions.stop: Perihilar opacities are identified and distinguished from focal consolidation or diffuse reticular patterns.

actions.observe: Compare Figure 2 lung fields against Figure 1 to verify complete clearance of opacities and restoration of normal vascular markings.
actions.when: Question requires assessing evolution or resolution between two timepoints.
actions.stop: Visual confirmation that Figure 2 lacks the opacities seen in Figure 1, supporting 'complete resolution' over 'partial resolution' or 'progression'.

items.avoid: Inferring severity changes from classifier score differences (e.g., 0.94 vs null); assuming 'no strong finding' implies normality without visual verification; misidentifying perihilar edema as lower lobe consolidation.
items.source_evidence: Old models correctly identified resolution but relied on classifier scores (0.94 opacity in Fig 1, none in Fig 2) which are uncalibrated. The correction confirms Figure 1 shows bilateral perihilar fluffy opacities (pulmonary edema) and Figure 2 shows complete resolution. Visual inspection is required to distinguish 'perihilar fluffy opacities' from 'lower lobe consolidation' or 'diffuse reticular opacities' and to confirm 'complete' rather than 'partial' resolution, as tool scores cannot quantify extent or pattern.

items.topic: Blunt aortic injury signs: mediastinal widening and subpulmonary pneumothorax

actions.observe: Superior mediastinum width relative to thoracic diameter; check for loss of aortic knob definition or apical cap opacity suggesting hematoma.
actions.when: Question mentions blunt trauma/crush mechanism and asks for vascular injury indicators.
actions.stop: Mediastinal widening is visually confirmed or definitively ruled out by normal contour/width.

actions.observe: Costophrenic angles and hemidiaphragm contours for deep sulcus sign or elevated/domed appearance indicating subpulmonary pneumothorax.
actions.when: Evaluating options combining mediastinal findings with pleural space pathology.
actions.stop: Subpulmonary air collection is identified or excluded based on diaphragm shape and lung edge visibility.

items.avoid: Relying on chest_xray_report_generator claims of 'normal mediastinal contours' or 'no pneumothorax' when visual inspection suggests widening or subpulmonary air in trauma context; do not assume pediatric thymus explains widening in crush accidents without verifying vascular silhouette.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions incorrectly selected 'Bilateral pulmonary contusions' or relied on tool reports stating normal mediastinum. Released correct answers consistently identify 'Mediastinal widening with bilateral subpulmonary pneumothoraces' and 'Blunt aortic injury'. Visual evidence in Figure 1a shows widened superior mediastinum and obscured diaphragmatic contours consistent with subpulmonary pneumothorax, contradicting the automated report's 'normal limits' assertion. Uncertainty lies in distinguishing traumatic widening from technical factors, but trauma history prioritizes vascular injury assessment.

items.topic: Pulmonary aplasia vs atelectasis differentiation via compensatory hyperinflation

actions.observe: Inspect the contralateral (right) lung field for signs of overinflation, specifically increased radiolucency and flattened hemidiaphragm, which indicates compensatory hyperplasia/hyperinflation typical of pulmonary aplasia rather than simple volume loss.
actions.when: Evaluating a unilateral opaque or absent hemithorax to distinguish congenital absence from acquired collapse.
actions.stop: When clear evidence of contralateral hyperinflation (radiolucency > normal side, low diaphragm) is identified alongside ipsilateral opacity/absence.

actions.observe: Verify mediastinal shift direction and diaphragm position on the affected side; in aplasia, the mediastinum shifts toward the empty side, but the key discriminator against atelectasis is the healthy lung's expansion into the space.
actions.when: Differentiating between total atelectasis (where the remaining lung is usually normal size or compressed) and aplasia (where the remaining lung is hypertrophied).
actions.stop: Once the relationship between the opaque side and the lucency of the opposite side is established.

items.avoid: Selecting 'Absence of the left pulmonary artery' as the primary CXR finding; while anatomically true for aplasia, it is a vascular detail often invisible on plain film compared to the gross parenchymal change of contralateral overinflation. Do not rely on classifier scores for 'no strong finding' as this implies abnormality in this context.
items.source_evidence: The model previously selected 'Absence of the left pulmonary artery', but the reference answer is 'Right lung radiolucency due to overinflation'. The source images show a completely opaque left hemithorax with mediastinal shift to the left, but crucially, the right lung appears hyperlucent and expanded, filling the upper chest. This compensatory overinflation is the most reliable radiographic sign distinguishing aplasia (congenital absence allowing growth of the other lung) from acquired atelectasis (where the other lung remains normal size). The classifier returned no strong findings, which aligns with the limitation that 'no strong finding' does not mean normal; here it signifies a complex structural anomaly not captured by standard pathology tags.

items.topic: Asymptomatic foreign body in right hilum with longitudinal bronchial alignment

actions.observe: Right hilar region for a discrete high-density linear or tubular opacity aligned parallel to the bronchial tree axis.
actions.when: Question asks for location and characteristics of a foreign body or explains lack of symptoms.
actions.stop: High-density object is identified in the right hilum with orientation matching the bronchus; verify absence of distal atelectasis or air trapping to confirm non-obstructive nature.

actions.observe: Lung fields distal to the right hilum (right middle/lower zones) for signs of obstruction like consolidation, collapse, or hyperinflation.
actions.when: Confirming why the foreign body was asymptomatic or unnoticed.
actions.stop: Distal lung parenchyma appears clear/aerated, supporting the conclusion that the object's alignment permitted normal air passage.

items.avoid: Inferring obstruction or symptoms solely from the presence of a foreign body; assuming low density implies soft tissue without verifying radiopacity; misidentifying the left hilum as the location when the density is clearly right-sided.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions correctly identified the right hilum location and high-density nature but varied slightly in phrasing regarding 'longitudinal alignment'. The reference answer confirms the foreign body is in the right hilum, is high-density, and its alignment with the bronchus allowed normal air passage, preventing symptoms. Visual evidence in Figure 3 shows a faint vertical density in the right perihilar region consistent with a longitudinally oriented object. Figure 6 (endoscopy) confirms a tubular structure within the airway, validating the 'alignment' hypothesis for asymptomatic presentation. Tools provided conflicting/irrelevant data (pneumonia scores, edema report) which should be ignored in favor of direct visual inspection of the hilar density and its orientation.

items.topic: Takayasu arteritis pulmonary vascular signs

actions.observe: Right hilar region and right lung field for vessel caliber asymmetry (small/absent right PA branch) and focal oligemia (Westermark sign).
actions.when: Question mentions Takayasu arteritis and asks for radiographic explanation of hemithorax appearance.
actions.stop: Asymmetry in hilar vessel size or focal lucency in right lung is identified; do not rely on 'clear lungs' report.

items.avoid: Accepting automated report claims of 'normal mediastinal/hilar contours' or 'clear lungs' which miss subtle vascular occlusion; assuming opacity implies pneumonia rather than vascular etiology.
items.source_evidence: Old model predicted compensatory left PA hypertrophy based on general patterns. Correct answer identifies subtle Westermark sign (focal oligemia) indicating chronic right PA obstruction. Source Figure 2a shows asymmetric right hilum/vascularity compared to left, consistent with Takayasu's, despite classifier scoring 'Lung Opacity' and report claiming normality. Visual inspection of vessel caliber is required over text generation.

items.topic: mediastinal mass vs lobar collapse resolution on serial CXR

actions.observe: Compare mediastinal width and contour in Figure 1a (pre) vs Figure 1b (post); check if the widened left mediastinal silhouette has normalized to a sharp vascular border.
actions.when: Question asks for cause of symptom improvement based on follow-up X-ray changes.
actions.stop: Visual confirmation that the mediastinal mass opacity has cleared completely in the follow-up image.

actions.observe: Inspect left lower lung zone in Figure 1a for dense opacity/loss of hemidiaphragm (collapse) vs Figure 1b for re-aeration; determine if residual atelectasis persists despite mass clearance.
actions.when: Distinguishing between 'resolution of collapse' and 'clearance of mass' as the primary driver of improvement.
actions.stop: Identification that while the mass is gone, some linear density or volume loss may remain, making 'mass clearance' the more accurate description of the major change.

items.avoid: Assuming that because the lung looks clearer, the collapse has fully resolved; do not conflate re-expansion with complete normalization if subtle atelectasis remains. Do not rely on single-image report generators for temporal comparisons.
items.source_evidence: Previous answer incorrectly identified 'Resolution of the left lower lobe collapse' as the primary reason for improvement. Reference answer corrects this to 'Clearance of the mediastinal mass'. Visual evidence in Figure 1a shows a massive left mediastinal opacity causing shift/collapse, while Figure 1b shows near-complete resolution of this mass with only minor residual findings, indicating the mass clearance was the dominant change.

items.topic: COP radiographic pattern: peripheral middle/lower zone consolidation

actions.observe: Inspect lung parenchyma for patchy airspace opacities specifically located at the periphery (subpleural) of the middle and lower lung zones, sparing the upper zones and central hila.
actions.when: Question asks for diagnosis based on CXR pattern or describes consolidation distribution in a patient with subacute symptoms unresponsive to antibiotics.
actions.stop: Peripheral middle/lower zone consolidations are visually confirmed; do not rely on classifier scores which may miss this specific pattern.

actions.observe: Verify absence of dominant upper lobe cavitation, hilar lymphadenopathy, or diffuse reticular fibrosis to distinguish from TB, sarcoidosis, or IPF.
actions.when: Differentiating COP from other interstitial or granulomatous diseases based on distribution.
actions.stop: Pattern matches peripheral/basal predominance without upper lobe dominance or fibrotic honeycombing.

items.avoid: Trusting chest_xray_classifier 'no strong findings' or report generator 'no focal consolidation' outputs, as these tools frequently fail to detect the subtle, patchy peripheral opacities characteristic of COP. Do not assume normalcy from tool silence.
items.source_evidence: Old model predictions and tool observations (classifier/report generator) incorrectly suggested normal findings or failed to identify pathology. Released correct answers consistently identify 'Idiopathic Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)' characterized by 'bilateral areas of airspace consolidation at the periphery of the middle and lower lung zones'. The visual evidence in Figure 1 confirms patchy opacities in these specific regions, contradicting the automated tool reports.

items.topic: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) pattern recognition in Tuberous Sclerosis

actions.observe: Inspect lung fields for diffuse, bilateral reticular or reticulonodular opacities distributed throughout all zones without focal consolidation.
actions.when: Question mentions tuberous sclerosis and asks to characterize pulmonary findings.
actions.stop: Diffuse bilateral reticular pattern is confirmed visually; do not rely on classifier scores which may mislabel as generic opacity.

actions.observe: Verify absence of cardiomegaly, pleural effusion, or lobar consolidation to exclude heart failure and pneumonia.
actions.when: Differentiating LAM from edema or infection based on distribution and associated signs.
actions.stop: Normal heart size and clear costophrenic angles support interstitial etiology over vascular/infectious causes.

items.avoid: Accepting 'diffuse nodular opacities consistent with metastatic disease' from the report generator when the visual pattern is reticular/interstitial and context is Tuberous Sclerosis; ignoring the specific clinical association between TS and LAM.
items.source_evidence: Old model claim: Report generator described 'diffuse nodular opacities, consistent with metastatic disease'. Released correction: Findings are 'Bilateral reticular shadowing indicative of lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)'. Supporting source observation: Image shows diffuse bilateral reticular markings without discrete nodules or masses. Uncertainty: Classifier flagged 'Lung Opacity' (0.86) but lacks specificity for interstitial patterns; report generator hallucinated metastases despite normal hilar contours.

items.topic: Differentiating pulmonary edema from pneumonia/atelectasis via perihilar distribution and valve prosthesis position

actions.observe: Inspect the central lung zones (perihilar regions) for symmetric, fluffy alveolar opacities extending outward from the hila, distinguishing this 'bat-wing' pattern of edema from peripheral or lobar consolidations typical of pneumonia.
actions.when: Evaluating bilateral lung opacities in a patient with cardiac history or hardware to distinguish edema from infection.
actions.stop: When the distribution is confirmed as predominantly perihilar/central rather than peripheral/lobar.

actions.observe: Examine the mediastinum and cardiac silhouette specifically for the radiopaque ring of an aortic valve prosthesis; assess if its position is atypical, tilted, or displaced relative to the expected anatomical axis.
actions.when: Options link respiratory symptoms to mechanical valve dysfunction or displacement.
actions.stop: When the prosthesis location is verified as normal or abnormal and correlated with the presence of pulmonary edema.

items.avoid: Relying on automated report generators that may falsely deny effusions or edema despite visible findings; do not assume peripheral consolidation implies pneumonia without checking for central/perihilar predominance.
items.source_evidence: Old models frequently selected 'pneumonia' or 'atelectasis' based on generic opacity detection. The reference answer corrects this to 'pulmonary edema due to cardiac failure' (specifically valve dislocation). Visual evidence shows bilateral perihilar alveolar consolidations and an aortic valve prosthesis. The key discriminant is the specific perihilar distribution of opacities combined with the assessment of the prosthetic valve's position, which automated tools often miss or misreport.

items.topic: Intracystic vessel vs artifact in lung cyst

actions.observe: Inspect the band-like opacity within the cystic lesion for continuity with hilar or peripheral pulmonary vasculature and consistent tubular caliber.
actions.when: Evaluating a linear density inside a radiolucent lung mass to distinguish vessel from artifact.
actions.stop: Opacity clearly tracks into normal vascular tree or is confirmed as non-anatomic superimposition.

items.avoid: Classifying intracystic linear opacities as shadow artifacts without verifying vascular continuity; assuming single-image report generators can identify specific internal cyst structures.
items.source_evidence: Old model predicted 'shadow artifact' for band-like structure in cyst. Reference answer corrected this to 'dilated blood vessel'. Source image (Fig 1c) shows arrows pointing to a distinct linear density traversing the upper third of a cystic area. The skill is to visually verify if such bands connect to the pulmonary vasculature, confirming them as vessels rather than overlapping shadows, which tools failed to identify.

items.topic: Constrictive calcified pericarditis vs valvular/ventricular calcification

actions.observe: Inspect the lateral view (Figure 1b) specifically for curvilinear or eggshell calcifications outlining the anterior and inferior cardiac borders (pericardium), distinct from the dense focal opacity of the pacemaker generator.
actions.when: Evaluating options involving pericardial disease versus intracardiac pathology in a patient with a pacemaker.
actions.stop: When linear calcifications are confirmed tracing the heart contour on the lateral view, distinguishing them from the discrete pacemaker device.

actions.observe: Verify pacemaker lead termination points on the frontal view to confirm right-sided placement (RA/RV), ruling out options suggesting left ventricular pacing or misalignment.
actions.when: Differentiating between constrictive pericarditis with standard pacing vs. anomalous lead placement.
actions.stop: Once lead trajectory is traced to the right heart chambers and pericardial calcification pattern is established.

items.avoid: Mistaking the high-density pacemaker generator or leads for pathological cardiac calcification; assuming calcification is valvular (mitral/aortic) without seeing specific annular location; ignoring the lateral view which is critical for visualizing pericardial shell calcification.
items.source_evidence: Old models generated reports mentioning pacemakers but failed to identify the diagnostic pericardial calcifications, likely distracted by the device. The correct answer relies on identifying 'calcifications predominantly over the right ventricle and atrioventricular grooves' (pericardial distribution) visible on the lateral view, combined with confirming the pacemaker is in the right ventricle to support the specific diagnosis of constrictive calcified pericarditis.

items.topic: Longitudinal comparison of pulmonary consolidation patterns (migratory infiltrates)

actions.observe: Inspect Figure 1 for the specific location and extent of consolidation (e.g., left upper lobe vs. diffuse left lung) and compare directly with Figure 2 to verify resolution of the original opacity and identify new opacities in distinct lobes (e.g., right upper lobe, left lower lobe).
actions.when: Question explicitly references two timepoints (Figure 1/Figure 2) and asks for progression or change.
actions.stop: When the spatial distribution of opacities in both images is mapped and the pattern of 'old resolving + new appearing elsewhere' is confirmed visually.

actions.observe: Verify that the new consolidations in Figure 2 are anatomically distinct from the resolved area in Figure 1 to support a 'migratory' pattern rather than simple expansion or persistence.
actions.when: Evaluating options describing migration versus progression/worsening.
actions.stop: When the non-contiguous nature of the new findings relative to the old findings is established.

items.avoid: Inferring longitudinal change from single-image classifier scores or report generator outputs; assuming 'no strong finding' implies normality; relying on image filename order instead of explicit question binding for chronology.
items.source_evidence: Old models failed to correctly identify the migratory pattern of Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP), often misinterpreting the resolution of left-sided consolidation and appearance of right-sided/new left lower lobe consolidation. The released correct answers consistently describe the resolution of initial left lung consolidation and the emergence of new consolidations in the right upper lobe and/or left lower lobe. This confirms that accurate diagnosis requires direct visual comparison of the two provided figures to track the specific anatomical shift of opacities, which automated tools failed to capture.

items.topic: Pulmonary Langerhans' Cell Histiocytosis (PLCH) radiographic distribution and sparing patterns

actions.observe: Inspect the costophrenic angles and the medial aspect of the right middle lobe (adjacent to the right heart border) for relative sparing of reticulonodular opacities compared to the upper/mid lung zones.
actions.when: Evaluating a chest X-ray with diffuse nodular or reticulonodular opacities to distinguish PLCH from other interstitial lung diseases.
actions.stop: When clear visualization confirms preservation of lucency in the costophrenic angles and medial RML despite extensive disease elsewhere.

actions.observe: Assess the vertical distribution of the reticulonodular pattern to determine if it is predominantly upper/mid-zone versus lower-zone.
actions.when: Differentiating PLCH (upper/mid predominance) from conditions like IPF or aspiration (lower predominance).
actions.stop: When the zonal predominance is clearly established as upper/mid or lower.

items.avoid: Relying on automated report generators that may misclassify PLCH nodules/cysts as 'metastatic disease' or miss the specific sparing pattern; assuming bilateral symmetry implies non-PLCH (PLCH can be asymmetric); ignoring the medial RML sparing sign which is highly specific for PLCH.
items.source_evidence: Old models frequently misdiagnosed PLCH as metastatic disease or lymphangioleiomyomatosis due to failure to recognize the characteristic 'sparing of the costophrenic angles and medial tip of the right middle lobe'. The released correct answers consistently identify this specific distribution pattern (upper/mid zone predominance with basal/medial sparing) as the key discriminator for PLCH. Tool observations (classifier scores for edema/effusion/pneumonia) were often misleading or irrelevant to the specific interstitial pattern required for diagnosis.

items.topic: Kartagener syndrome: dextrocardia and left-sided horizontal fissure (situs inversus)

actions.observe: Cardiac apex position relative to midline; confirm if pointing to patient's right (dextrocardia).
actions.when: Evaluating options involving heart orientation or situs inversus.
actions.stop: Apex clearly points to the right hemithorax.

actions.observe: Horizontal fissure location; verify if present in the left hemithorax (mirror image of normal right-sided fissure).
actions.when: Distinguishing between normal anatomy and situs inversus patterns.
actions.stop: Fissure is visualized on the left side, confirming mirror-image anatomy.

items.avoid: Relying on automated report generators that may default to 'normal cardiomediastinal silhouette' despite obvious dextrocardia; assuming bronchiectasis must be visible on CXR to diagnose Kartagener's when situs inversus is the primary radiographic clue.
items.source_evidence: Old models and tools frequently missed dextrocardia or misidentified fissure laterality. The chest_xray_report_generator incorrectly stated 'cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal' for a case with clear dextrocardia. Correct answers consistently link Kartagener syndrome to the combination of a right-sided heart apex and a left-sided horizontal fissure (situs inversus), supported by clinical history of sinusitis/infections. Visual inspection confirms the heart shadow is on the right and the horizontal fissure is on the left.

items.topic: BOOP consolidation morphology and lymph node status

actions.observe: Left lower lobe (specifically apical/superior segment) for ill-defined, patchy parenchymal consolidation with air bronchograms or bronchial narrowing.
actions.when: Evaluating options distinguishing BOOP from malignancy, TB, or resolving pneumonia.
actions.stop: Ill-defined LLL consolidation is confirmed AND hilar/mediastinal contours are visually normal (no lymphadenopathy).

actions.observe: Hilar and mediastinal contours to verify absence of lymphadenopathy.
actions.when: Differentiating BOOP (typically no adenopathy) from Sarcoidosis, TB, or Malignancy.
actions.stop: Contours are smooth and non-bulging; no discrete masses or lobulated hilar shadows seen.

items.avoid: Relying on chest_xray_classifier scores (unreliable for this pattern) or report_generator claims of 'clear lungs' which contradict the visible LLL opacity. Do not assume lymphadenopathy is present without distinct hilar bulging.
items.source_evidence: Old models failed to identify the specific LLL consolidation or incorrectly reported clear lungs/normal findings via tools. The correct answer requires identifying an ill-defined consolidation in the apical segment of the left lower lobe with bronchial narrowing and explicitly noting the ABSENCE of lymphadenopathy to support BOOP over TB/Malignancy. Visual inspection of Figure 1a/1b confirms the LLL opacity and normal hila, contradicting automated tool outputs.

items.topic: Differentiating restrictive vs obstructive patterns via lung volume assessment in interstitial disease

actions.observe: Assess lung volumes by counting posterior ribs above the diaphragm and checking diaphragm position (flat vs elevated) to distinguish hyperinflation from restriction.
actions.when: Evaluating options linking interstitial changes to lung volume status (high vs low).
actions.stop: When rib count confirms volume status (e.g., <9 posterior ribs suggests low volume/restriction; >10 suggests hyperinflation).

actions.observe: Inspect lung parenchyma for diffuse reticular or nodular opacities consistent with interstitial changes, verifying they are not absent.
actions.when: Confirming the presence of interstitial pathology required by all valid options.
actions.stop: When diffuse interstitial markings are visually confirmed against clear lung fields.

items.avoid: Assuming interstitial changes imply obstruction or high lung volumes; do not rely on classifier scores for volume assessment as they do not measure geometry.
items.source_evidence: Old model incorrectly selected 'high lung volumes/obstructive' despite reference confirming 'low lung volumes/restrictive'. The source image shows reduced lung volumes (elevated hemidiaphragms, limited rib count) with diffuse interstitial markings. This contradicts the old claim of hyperinflation. Uncertainty lies in distinguishing subtle volume loss from normal variation without explicit rib counting.

items.topic: Kartagener's syndrome radiographic signs: dextrocardia and bibasilar bronchiectasis

actions.observe: Cardiac apex and gastric bubble location to confirm dextrocardia/situs inversus (apex points right, bubble on right).
actions.when: Question mentions Kartagener's syndrome or situs inversus.
actions.stop: Dextrocardia is visually confirmed or ruled out.

actions.observe: Lung bases for increased reticular markings, tram-tracking, or ring shadows indicating bronchiectasis, specifically checking if changes are bilateral and basilar.
actions.when: Evaluating options regarding bronchiectasis distribution in Kartagener's.
actions.stop: Basilar opacities consistent with bronchiectasis are identified or excluded.

items.avoid: Selecting 'Left-sided liver and right-sided heart' as the primary finding supporting diagnosis when 'Bibasilar bronchiectasis' is an option; while situs inversus is present, bronchiectasis is the specific pulmonary pathology defining the syndrome's respiratory presentation in this context. Also avoid assuming upper lobe predominance (typical of CF) rather than lower lobe/basal predominance typical of PCD/Kartagener's.
items.source_evidence: Old model predicted 'Left-sided liver and right-sided heart' for the finding supporting Kartagener's diagnosis. Reference answer corrected this to 'Bibasilar bronchiectasis'. Source images (Figure 4) show dextrocardia (apex right) and prominent basal markings. The correction emphasizes that while situs inversus is a component, the question specifically targeted the bronchiectatic finding (bibasilar) which distinguishes the pulmonary manifestation, whereas the old answer focused solely on organ arrangement. Uncertainty exists in distinguishing subtle bronchiectasis from consolidation without CT, but the basal distribution is the key discriminator against upper-lobe diseases.
